1	\section{Experiments}
2	
3	\subsection{Setup}
4	
5	We test on synthetic ($N{=}5{,}000$, $K \in \{2, 4\}$, controlled $\Delta\tau$ and $\Delta\pi$, 100 MC runs) and semi-synthetic (TweetEval sentiment~\cite{barbieri2020tweeteval}, $K{=}4$ unbalanced subgroups, $\pi \in \{0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.25\}$) DGPs; full specifications in Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}.
6	
7	We compare: (1) \textit{Naive} (no correction), (2) \textit{Global} (pooled confusion matrix, equivalent to PPI/DSL~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi,egami2024dsl} with homogeneous error), (3) \textit{Stratified MLE} (per-subgroup DSL without shrinkage), (4) \textit{HB EC-HTE} (our method), (5) \textit{PPCI}~\cite{sui2026ppci}, and (6) \textit{EC-HTE+PPCI}.
8	For CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal}, we compare naive, global, and EC-HTE variants.
9	Primary metrics are $|\text{bias}|$, RMSE, and 95\% CI coverage, averaged across subgroups and 100 MC runs.
10	Robustness validation covers hate speech, six OpenAI models, subgroup misspecification, asymmetric confusion matrices, confounded treatment, and outcome-dependent misclassification (all $\geq$93.5\% coverage; Appendices~\ref{app:hatespeech}--\ref{app:a1_sensitivity}).
11	
12	\subsection{Empirical Validation of the Bias Identity}
13	\label{sec:bias_mechanism}
14	
15	We verify Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} on a $K{=}2$ grid (520 configurations, $\Delta\pi \in [0, 0.25]$, $\Delta\tau \in (0, 0.50]$) and a $K{=}4$ grid (Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}).
16	Regressing observed subgroup bias on $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1{-}2\bar{\pi})$ yields $R^2 = 0.994$ ($K{=}2$) and $0.974$ ($K{=}4$); residual variance reflects MC noise ($R^2 \geq 0.976$ even at $P(Z{=}1) = 0.1$; Appendix~\ref{app:classimbalance}).
17	Global correction worsens bias in 50\% of $K{=}2$ configurations (260/520, excluding $\Delta\pi{=}0$), with amplification reaching 2.86$\times$ ($K{=}2$) and 2.41$\times$ ($K{=}4$); Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} visualizes the amplification surface.
18	Beyond amplification, global correction reverses the sign of the estimated treatment effect for at least one subgroup in 92\% of configurations (500/546, 50\% of all subgroup-rows), with all eight real LLMs exhibiting the same pattern (49\%); EC-HTE eliminates sign reversal entirely (Figure~\ref{fig:sign_reversal}).
19	
20	\begin{figure*}[t]
21	\centering
22	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig2_heatmap.pdf}
23	\caption{Bias amplification under global correction ($K{=}2$). (a) Low-error subgroup: correction always helps. (b) High-error subgroup: correction \emph{increases} bias when $\Delta\pi > 0.12$ (hatched), reaching 2.86$\times$.}
24	\label{fig:heatmap}
25	\end{figure*}
26	
27	\subsection{EC-HTE Evaluation}
28	\label{sec:ec_hte_eval}
29	
30	Table~\ref{tab:main_results} presents the main results across representative configurations.
31	In the $K{=}2$ extreme row, global correction \emph{increases} $|\text{bias}|$ relative to naive (0.059 vs.\ 0.058), confirming the over-correction mechanism of Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}.
32	F-L scalar correction ($\hat{\tau}/(1{-}2\bar{\pi})$) increases $|\text{bias}|$ to 0.122 with coverage 0.68---worse than naive---because a single scalar cannot correct heterogeneous attenuation; F-L per-subgroup inflates bias to 0.168 as $(1{-}2\pi_s) \to 0$ (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}).
33	HB EC-HTE reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 to 0.008 (7.4$\times$) at $K{=}2$ and from 0.056 to 0.012 (4.7$\times$) at $K{=}4$, maintaining near-nominal coverage (0.94--0.96) with lower RMSE than stratified MLE.
34	Under moderate heterogeneity ($K{=}2$) and in the semi-synthetic TweetEval experiment ($K{=}4$, $n_{\text{expert}}{=}250$), methods converge: EC-HTE and global achieve comparable bias ($p > 0.05$), though EC-HTE incurs higher RMSE when $\Delta\pi$ or per-subgroup budget is marginal (Table~\ref{tab:main_supp}).
35	
36	\paragraph{CausalForest.}
37	With CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal} ($K{=}4$, extreme, $n{=}500$), EC-HTE reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.191 to 0.039 (4.9$\times$), improving coverage from 0.58 to 0.90; global correction amplifies naive bias up to 5.9$\times$ because the forest magnifies label errors (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}).
38	The residual coverage gap (90\% vs.\ oracle 94--96\%) reflects $M^{-1}$ SE propagation; a full bootstrap corrects this (Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_se}).
39	
40	\begin{table}[t]
41	\centering
42	\caption{Main results (extreme heterogeneity). Metrics averaged over subgroups, $z$-levels, 100 MC runs. Bold: lowest $|\text{bias}|$. $^\dagger$RMSE exceeds Global. Moderate heterogeneity and TweetEval results---where methods converge and EC-HTE RMSE exceeds Global---in Table~\ref{tab:main_supp}; MC SEs in Appendix~\ref{app:mcse}.}
43	\label{tab:main_results}
44	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
45	\begin{tabular}{ll ccc}
46	\toprule
47	Configuration & Method & $|\text{Bias}|$ & RMSE & 95\% CI Cov. \\
48	\midrule
49	\multirow{6}{*}{\shortstack[l]{DIM\\$K{=}2$, $n{=}250$}}
50	 & Naive & 0.058 & 0.090 & 0.82 \\
51	 & Global & 0.059 & 0.099 & 0.87 \\
52	 & F-L Scalar & 0.122 & 0.159 & 0.68 \\
53	 & F-L Per-sub. & 0.168 & 0.220 & 0.65 \\
54	 & Strat.\ MLE & 0.012 & 0.094 & 0.95 \\
55	 & HB EC-HTE & \textbf{0.008} & 0.089 & 0.94 \\
56	\midrule
57	\multirow{4}{*}{\shortstack[l]{DIM\\$K{=}4$, $n{=}500$}}
58	 & Naive & 0.062 & 0.113 & 0.88 \\
59	 & Global & 0.056 & 0.125 & 0.91 \\
60	 & Strat.\ MLE & \textbf{0.010} & 0.127$^\dagger$ & 0.95 \\
61	 & HB EC-HTE & 0.012 & 0.120 & 0.96 \\
62	\midrule
63	\multirow{3}{*}{\shortstack[l]{CausalForest\\$K{=}4$, $n{=}500$}}
64	 & Naive & 0.208 & 0.231 & 0.44 \\
65	 & Global & 0.191 & 0.244 & 0.58 \\
66	 & EC-HTE Forest & \textbf{0.039} & 0.180 & 0.90 \\
67	\bottomrule
68	\end{tabular}}
69	\end{table}
70	
71	\subsection{Actionable Diagnostic Without EC-HTE}
72	\label{sec:diagnostic}
73	
74	Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts} provides a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic: global correction increases bias in subgroup $s$ iff $|\delta_s| / ((1-2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s) > 1$, computable from a pilot sample without estimating treatment effects.
75	A threshold classifier achieves AUC = 0.86 at the subgroup level (Figure~\ref{fig:roc}, Appendix).
76	On real LLM confusion matrices (16 combinations; Appendix~\ref{app:screening}), AUC drops to 0.63; restricting to subgroups with $\tau_s > 0$ recovers AUC $= 1.0$.
77	For $K{=}2$, $|\delta_0|{=}|\delta_1|$ limits discrimination; a meta-criterion ($\max_s \mathrm{score}(s) > 1$) recovers reliability (AUC $\geq 0.75$) for $K{\geq}4$, while $\max_s \mathrm{score}(s) \leq 1$ signals unreliable regimes (Appendix~\ref{app:screening}).
78	
79	The condition number $\kappa(\hat{C}_s)$ governs correction at three levels: $\kappa > 100$ triggers the singularity guard; $\kappa \leq 1.25$ guarantees strongest bias reduction; $\kappa \in (1.25, 3]$---covering all 13 tested LLM--dataset combinations---maintains calibrated coverage ($\geq$93\% vs.\ Global 86--91\%) with RMSE gains at $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 500$ (Appendix~\ref{app:kappa_analysis}).
80	Budget crossover curves, $K{=}8$ scalability, and multi-LLM validation ($R^2 = 0.975$) appear in Appendices~\ref{sec:budget}--\ref{app:multilm}.

1	\section*{Limitations}
2	\label{sec:limitations}
3	
4	EC-HTE requires $n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ per subgroup for stable hierarchical Bayesian estimation.
5	For $K{=}2$, EC-HTE remains effective even at $P(Z{=}1) = 0.1$ (Appendix~\ref{app:classimbalance}); for $K{=}4$, $P(Z{=}1) \geq 0.3$ is needed to approach breakeven with global correction at $n_{\text{expert}}{=}250$.
6	Even above this threshold, stratification incurs a variance cost: at $K{=}4$, extreme heterogeneity, and $n_{\text{expert}} \leq 100$, CausalForest RMSE reaches 3.5$\times$ that of the naive estimator.
7	The method also requires moderate baseline classifier accuracy per subgroup; when any subgroup's FNR or FPR approaches 0.5, the confusion matrix row approaches a uniform distribution and inversion amplifies noise (Appendix~\ref{app:semireal}), as confirmed independently in the hate speech case study (Appendix~\ref{app:hatespeech}).
8	These failure modes interact: high per-subgroup error-rate variance combined with low minority prevalence $P(Z{=}1)$ jointly reduces effective per-subgroup expert labels for the positive class, compounding both sources of estimation error.
9	Additionally, our main semi-synthetic experiments use constant treatment effects across subgroups; a supplementary heterogeneous-$\tau$ DGP (Appendix~\ref{app:multilm_opensource}) shows that EC-HTE achieves targeted bias and RMSE improvement in subgroups with large $\Delta\tau$, though aggregate RMSE remains comparable to global correction.
10	At $K{=}8$ with $n_{\text{expert}}{=}250$ (${\approx}31$ labels/subgroup), EC-HTE maintains nominal coverage (95.6\%) but RMSE exceeds global correction, establishing $K{=}8$ as a scalability boundary under fixed budget (Appendix~\ref{app:k8_subgroups}).
11	The hierarchical prior implicitly performs soft merging---subgroups with insufficient data are shrunk toward the global estimate---but explicit hierarchical subgroup merging or adaptive budget allocation may extend the applicability frontier beyond $K{=}8$; we leave these extensions to future work.
12	
13	Assumption~(A1) (conditional independence of misclassification and potential outcomes) is not empirically testable.
14	When LLM accuracy correlates with outcome magnitude---e.g., extreme sentiment is both easier to classify and associated with larger treatment effects---Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} acquires an $O(\gamma)$ perturbation (Section~\ref{sec:theory}).
15	Sensitivity simulation (Appendix~\ref{app:a1_sensitivity}) shows that EC-HTE maintains near-nominal coverage ($\geq$93.5\%) under outcome-dependent misclassification up to $\gamma = 0.2$, with bias increasing only 13.7\%; developing a formal closed-form bound for the $O(\gamma)$ perturbation remains a natural extension~\cite{lash2009applying,dorn2022sharp}.
16	Treatment-dependent misclassification ($P(\hat{Z} \mid Z, T) \neq P(\hat{Z} \mid Z)$), where LLM accuracy varies with treatment status, violates (A1) analogously; the $O(\gamma)$ perturbation structure applies symmetrically, and sensitivity analysis for this case is left to future work.
17	
18	Oracle experiments confirm CausalForest plug-in SE is well-calibrated (94--96\% coverage with true $Z$ labels); EC-HTE plug-in SE achieves 93.8\% aggregate coverage under standard hyperparameters ($n_{\text{estimators}}{=}200$), with residual under-coverage concentrated in high-error subgroups due to asymmetric $M^{-1}$ SE propagation.
19	A full bootstrap procedure ($B{=}100$; re-estimate CM and re-fit per replicate) recovers $\geq$95\% coverage across all expert budgets tested ($n_{\text{expert}} \in \{25, 50, 75, 100, 200\}$; Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_se}); even plug-in SE achieves $\geq$91\% at $n_{\text{expert}}{=}25$.
20	For the DIM estimator, plug-in SE achieves $\geq$95\% coverage across all budgets.
21	
22	The diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}) achieves AUC $= 0.86$ under synthetic symmetric errors but degrades to $0.63$ on real LLM confusion matrices (pooled across 16 model--dataset combinations; Appendix~\ref{app:screening}).
23	For $K{=}2$, the diagnostic anti-predicts because $|\delta_0|{=}|\delta_1|$ forces score differentiation onto $1/\pi_s$ alone, which inversely correlates with actual harm; for binary $Z$, the asymmetric $B_s$-based formulation (Remark~2) is algebraically equivalent and offers no improvement.
24	Performance is strongest for $K{\geq}4$ with moderate asymmetry (AUC $= 0.66$; Appendix~\ref{app:asymmetric}).
25	The diagnostic remains a theoretically grounded criterion---the bias identity's product structure ensures it correctly identifies the \emph{direction} of bias amplification---but should be paired with $R^2$ validation of the bias identity rather than used as a standalone screening rule.
26	
27	All main experiments use symmetric error rates and additive CATE injection ($Y(1) = Y(0) + \tau(Z)$).
28	The bias identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) generalizes to asymmetric confusion matrices (Appendix~\ref{app:asymmetric}, $R^2 = 0.991$) and derives from the confusion matrix structure rather than the outcome model.
29	While our main experiments use additive CATE injection, a supplementary experiment with multiplicative effects ($Y(1) = Y(0) \times \exp(\tau(Z))$) yields comparable bias reduction (52\%) and nominal coverage (0.955; Appendix~\ref{app:rlearner}), confirming robustness to the functional form of treatment effects.
30	EC-HTE further requires discrete, pre-defined subgroups; subgroup definitions should be pre-specified based on domain knowledge, as data-driven subgroup discovery risks overfitting the confusion matrix structure to sample-specific noise. Continuous effect modifiers or latent subgroup discovery settings require different approaches; discretizing a continuous modifier introduces grouping bias whose magnitude depends on bin width, and intersectional subgroups with many levels may exceed the $n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ budget threshold.
31	Our experiments define subgroups by text features (hashtag presence, text length); demographic subgroups---where prior work documents the most concerning disparities \citep{ashwin2025bias}---require sensitive data access beyond the scope of this study.
32	EC-HTE's correction mechanism is agnostic to subgroup definition: it corrects any per-subgroup confusion-matrix heterogeneity, whether defined by text features, demographics, or other covariates.
33	Ground-truth subgroup CATEs are unavailable in public datasets; classic causal inference benchmarks (e.g., LaLonde, IHDP) lack the LLM annotation step that creates the measurement error our method corrects, precluding direct application. We use synthetic CATE injection on real text features and real LLM annotations.
34	We leave full real-data validation---on a dataset combining RCT design, ground-truth CATEs, and LLM annotations---to future work as suitable public benchmarks become available.
35	Code and data generation scripts will be released upon acceptance.

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

EC-HTE requires $n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ per subgroup for stable hierarchical Bayesian estimation.
For $K{=}2$, EC-HTE remains effective even at $P(Z{=}1) = 0.1$ (Appendix~\ref{app:classimbalance}); for $K{=}4$, $P(Z{=}1) \geq 0.3$ is needed to approach breakeven with global correction at $n_{\text{expert}}{=}250$.
Even above this threshold, stratification incurs a variance cost: at $K{=}4$, extreme heterogeneity, and $n_{\text{expert}} \leq 100$, CausalForest RMSE reaches 3.5$\times$ that of the naive estimator.
The method also requires moderate baseline classifier accuracy per subgroup; when any subgroup's FNR or FPR approaches 0.5, the confusion matrix row approaches a uniform distribution and inversion amplifies noise (Appendix~\ref{app:semireal}), as confirmed independently in the hate speech case study (Appendix~\ref{app:hatespeech}).
These failure modes interact: high per-subgroup error-rate variance combined with low minority prevalence $P(Z{=}1)$ jointly reduces effective per-subgroup expert labels for the positive class, compounding both sources of estimation error.
Additionally, our main semi-synthetic experiments use constant treatment effects across subgroups; a supplementary heterogeneous-$\tau$ DGP (Appendix~\ref{app:multilm_opensource}) shows that EC-HTE achieves targeted bias and RMSE improvement in subgroups with large $\Delta\tau$, though aggregate RMSE remains comparable to global correction.
At $K{=}8$ with $n_{\text{expert}}{=}250$ (${\approx}31$ labels/subgroup), EC-HTE maintains nominal coverage (95.6\%) but RMSE exceeds global correction, establishing $K{=}8$ as a scalability boundary under fixed budget (Appendix~\ref{app:k8_subgroups}).
The hierarchical prior implicitly performs soft merging---subgroups with insufficient data are shrunk toward the global estimate---but explicit hierarchical subgroup merging or adaptive budget allocation may extend the applicability frontier beyond $K{=}8$; we leave these extensions to future work.

Assumption~(A1) (conditional independence of misclassification and potential outcomes) is not empirically testable.
When LLM accuracy correlates with outcome magnitude---e.g., extreme sentiment is both easier to classify and associated with larger treatment effects---Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} acquires an $O(\gamma)$ perturbation (Section~\ref{sec:theory}).
Sensitivity simulation (Appendix~\ref{app:a1_sensitivity}) shows that EC-HTE maintains near-nominal coverage ($\geq$93.5\%) under outcome-dependent misclassification up to $\gamma = 0.2$, with bias increasing only 13.7\%; developing a formal closed-form bound for the $O(\gamma)$ perturbation remains a natural extension~\cite{lash2009applying,dorn2022sharp}.
Treatment-dependent misclassification ($P(\hat{Z} \mid Z, T) \neq P(\hat{Z} \mid Z)$), where LLM accuracy varies with treatment status, violates (A1) analogously; the $O(\gamma)$ perturbation structure applies symmetrically, and sensitivity analysis for this case is left to future work.

Oracle experiments confirm CausalForest plug-in SE is well-calibrated (94--96\% coverage with true $Z$ labels); EC-HTE plug-in SE achieves 93.8\% aggregate coverage under standard hyperparameters ($n_{\text{estimators}}{=}200$), with residual under-coverage concentrated in high-error subgroups due to asymmetric $M^{-1}$ SE propagation.
A full bootstrap procedure ($B{=}100$; re-estimate CM and re-fit per replicate) recovers $\geq$95\% coverage across all expert budgets tested ($n_{\text{expert}} \in \{25, 50, 75, 100, 200\}$; Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_se}); even plug-in SE achieves $\geq$91\% at $n_{\text{expert}}{=}25$.
For the DIM estimator, plug-in SE achieves $\geq$95\% coverage across all budgets.

The diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}) achieves AUC $= 0.86$ under synthetic symmetric errors but degrades to $0.63$ on real LLM confusion matrices (pooled across 16 model--dataset combinations; Appendix~\ref{app:screening}).
For $K{=}2$, the diagnostic anti-predicts because $|\delta_0|{=}|\delta_1|$ forces score differentiation onto $1/\pi_s$ alone, which inversely correlates with actual harm; for binary $Z$, the asymmetric $B_s$-based formulation (Remark~2) is algebraically equivalent and offers no improvement.
Performance is strongest for $K{\geq}4$ with moderate asymmetry (AUC $= 0.66$; Appendix~\ref{app:asymmetric}).
The diagnostic remains a theoretically grounded criterion---the bias identity's product structure ensures it correctly identifies the \emph{direction} of bias amplification---but should be paired with $R^2$ validation of the bias identity rather than used as a standalone screening rule.

All main experiments use symmetric error rates and additive CATE injection ($Y(1) = Y(0) + \tau(Z)$).
The bias identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) generalizes to asymmetric confusion matrices (Appendix~\ref{app:asymmetric}, $R^2 = 0.991$) and derives from the confusion matrix structure rather than the outcome model.
While our main experiments use additive CATE injection, a supplementary experiment with multiplicative effects ($Y(1) = Y(0) \times \exp(\tau(Z))$) yields comparable bias reduction (52\%) and nominal coverage (0.955; Appendix~\ref{app:rlearner}), confirming robustness to the functional form of treatment effects.
EC-HTE further requires discrete, pre-defined subgroups; subgroup definitions should be pre-specified based on domain knowledge, as data-driven subgroup discovery risks overfitting the confusion matrix structure to sample-specific noise. Continuous effect modifiers or latent subgroup discovery settings require different approaches; discretizing a continuous modifier introduces grouping bias whose magnitude depends on bin width, and intersectional subgroups with many levels may exceed the $n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ budget threshold.
Our experiments define subgroups by text features (hashtag presence, text length); demographic subgroups---where prior work documents the most concerning disparities \citep{ashwin2025bias}---require sensitive data access beyond the scope of this study.
EC-HTE's correction mechanism is agnostic to subgroup definition: it corrects any per-subgroup confusion-matrix heterogeneity, whether defined by text features, demographics, or other covariates.
Ground-truth subgroup CATEs are unavailable in public datasets; classic causal inference benchmarks (e.g., LaLonde, IHDP) lack the LLM annotation step that creates the measurement error our method corrects, precluding direct application. We use synthetic CATE injection on real text features and real LLM annotations.
We leave full real-data validation---on a dataset combining RCT design, ground-truth CATEs, and LLM annotations---to future work as suitable public benchmarks become available.
Code and data generation scripts will be released upon acceptance.

1	\section{EC-HTE: Error-Corrected Heterogeneous Treatment Effects}
2	\label{sec:method}
3	
4	Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} identifies per-subgroup misclassification deviation as the bias source; the natural correction is per-subgroup confusion matrix inversion.
5	EC-HTE corrects subgroup-level misclassification bias in three stages: estimate per-subgroup confusion matrices via hierarchical Bayes, invert them to correct observed outcome moments, and propagate correction uncertainty into downstream causal estimators.
6	The complete procedure is summarized in Algorithm~\ref{alg:echte} (Appendix~\ref{app:algorithm}).
7	
8	\subsection{Hierarchical Bayes Confusion Matrix Estimation}
9	
10	We place a Dirichlet-Multinomial hierarchical model over the confusion matrices $\{C_s\}_{s=1}^K$.
11	For each subgroup $s$, row $j$ of $C_s$ has a Dirichlet prior centered at the global pooled confusion matrix $\hat{C}_{\text{global}}$: $\text{Dir}(\alpha_0 \cdot \hat{C}_{\text{global},j})$, where $\hat{C}_{\text{global},j}$ is the $j$-th row of the pooled CM and $\alpha_0 > 0$ is a shared concentration parameter estimated via empirical Bayes (marginal likelihood maximization).
12	Large $\alpha_0$ pulls subgroup estimates toward $\hat{C}_{\text{global}}$ (global correction), while small $\alpha_0$ allows subgroup-specific rates to dominate (stratified correction).
13	This partial pooling---a form of James-Stein shrinkage well-established in small-area estimation---borrows strength across subgroups when estimating confusion matrices from limited expert labels, reducing variance for small subgroups while preserving heterogeneity where data support it.
14	
15	Posterior inference uses Gibbs sampling (convergence diagnostics in Appendix~\ref{app:algorithm}).
16	HB estimation outperforms stratified MLE in 87.5\% of configurations (21 of 24) across the experimental grid (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}), with the largest gains when $n_{\text{expert}} / K < 100$.
17	The advantage requires $n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ per subgroup; below this threshold, stratified MLE is preferred because the hierarchical model lacks sufficient observations for stable shrinkage.
18	At $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 1000$, HB and stratified MLE converge to within 0.5\% on all metrics.
19	Sensitivity analysis shows $<$5\% RMSE variation under 2$\times$ hyperprior perturbation, confirming that results are not driven by prior specification.
20	
21	\subsection{Subgroup-Stratified Correction}
22	
23	Given posterior mean confusion matrices $\hat{C}_s$, we correct observed outcome moments per subgroup by matrix inversion:
24	\begin{equation}
25	\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s = \hat{C}_s^{-1} \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s,
26	\end{equation}
27	where $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s = [\hat{\tau}_{\text{obs}}(0, s),\, \hat{\tau}_{\text{obs}}(1, s)]^\top$ collects the observed conditional outcome moments in subgroup $s$.
28	This requires $\det(\hat{C}_s) \neq 0$ for all $s$, which holds under assumption~(A4) ($\pi_s \neq 0.5$) but may fail in finite samples when error rates approach degeneracy.
29	In practice, Laplace smoothing of the confusion matrix counts ensures finite-sample invertibility.
30	We impose a singularity guard: if the condition number $\kappa(\hat{C}_s) > 100$ (for a $2{\times}2$ symmetric confusion matrix, this corresponds to $\pi_s > 0.495$, i.e., near-random classification), subgroup $s$ falls back to global correction $\bar{C}^{-1}$; when the fallback triggers, the standard error computation also uses $\bar{C}^{-1}$ for that subgroup, ensuring consistency between point estimates and confidence intervals.
31	This hard guard prevents numerical catastrophe; $\kappa \leq 1.25$ is a sufficient condition for strongest bias reduction (Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}), though EC-HTE maintains calibrated coverage ($\geq$93\%) across the wider $\kappa \in [1.4, 3.0]$ range observed in practice (Appendix~\ref{app:kappa_analysis}).
32	
33	The contrast with global correction is direct.
34	Global correction applies $\bar{C}^{-1}$ uniformly to all subgroups, introducing the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ bias identified in Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}.
35	Subgroup-stratified correction eliminates this bias by matching each subgroup's correction to its own misclassification structure, at the cost of higher variance from estimating $K$ separate confusion matrices (Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}).
36	
37	\subsection{Variance-Adjusted CausalForest}
38	
39	For heterogeneous treatment effect estimation, we feed corrected covariates into CausalForestDML~\cite{wager2018causal} with honest splitting.
40	The forest produces per-observation standard error estimates $\text{se}_i$.
41	To account for confusion matrix correction, we propagate uncertainty through the inverse mapping:
42	\begin{equation}
43	\text{se}_{\text{corrected},i} = \sqrt{\text{diag}\!\left(\hat{C}_{S_i}^{-1}\, \text{diag}(\text{se}_i^2)\, \hat{C}_{S_i}^{-\top}\right)}.
44	\end{equation}
45	This plug-in SE conditions on $\hat{C}_s$, neglecting CM estimation uncertainty; at $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 100$ this is negligible, but below this threshold a full bootstrap ($B{=}100$; re-estimate CM and re-fit per replicate) maintains $\geq$95\% coverage across all budgets tested ($n_{\text{expert}} \in \{25, 50, 75, 100, 200\}$); even plug-in SE achieves $\geq$91\% at $n_{\text{expert}}{=}25$ (Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_se}).
46	When $n_{\text{expert}}/K < 50$, we recommend bootstrap SE; otherwise plug-in SE suffices.
47	
48	\paragraph{Diagnostic criterion.}
49	Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts} provides a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic: global correction harms subgroup $s$ if and only if $|\delta_s| / ((1-2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s) > 1$, a condition depending only on per-subgroup misclassification rates estimable from a pilot sample.
50	This breaks the circular dependency that would arise if the diagnostic required CATE estimates.
51	A threshold classifier achieves AUC~=~0.86 at the subgroup level, reaching 1.0 when restricted to subgroups with $\tau_s > 0$ (Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
52	
53	\paragraph{Composition with PPCI.}
54	EC-HTE corrects structured covariate misclassification through $\hat{C}_s^{-1}$ inversion but cannot address outcome-level measurement error.
55	PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} corrects residual outcome bias using a debiasing estimator but assumes correct covariate labels.
56	The two methods are complementary: apply EC-HTE first to correct covariate labels, then PPCI to correct outcome predictions.
57	Neither is redundant with the other: EC-HTE alone cannot fix outcome error, while PPCI alone incurs higher variance for covariate error.
58	Under both error types simultaneously, the composition reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.179 to 0.007 (Appendix~\ref{sec:ppci}).

\section{EC-HTE: Error-Corrected Heterogeneous Treatment Effects}
\label{sec:method}

Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} identifies per-subgroup misclassification deviation as the bias source; the natural correction is per-subgroup confusion matrix inversion.
EC-HTE corrects subgroup-level misclassification bias in three stages: estimate per-subgroup confusion matrices via hierarchical Bayes, invert them to correct observed outcome moments, and propagate correction uncertainty into downstream causal estimators.
The complete procedure is summarized in Algorithm~\ref{alg:echte} (Appendix~\ref{app:algorithm}).

\subsection{Hierarchical Bayes Confusion Matrix Estimation}

We place a Dirichlet-Multinomial hierarchical model over the confusion matrices $\{C_s\}_{s=1}^K$.
For each subgroup $s$, row $j$ of $C_s$ has a Dirichlet prior centered at the global pooled confusion matrix $\hat{C}_{\text{global}}$: $\text{Dir}(\alpha_0 \cdot \hat{C}_{\text{global},j})$, where $\hat{C}_{\text{global},j}$ is the $j$-th row of the pooled CM and $\alpha_0 > 0$ is a shared concentration parameter estimated via empirical Bayes (marginal likelihood maximization).
Large $\alpha_0$ pulls subgroup estimates toward $\hat{C}_{\text{global}}$ (global correction), while small $\alpha_0$ allows subgroup-specific rates to dominate (stratified correction).
This partial pooling---a form of James-Stein shrinkage well-established in small-area estimation---borrows strength across subgroups when estimating confusion matrices from limited expert labels, reducing variance for small subgroups while preserving heterogeneity where data support it.

Posterior inference uses Gibbs sampling (convergence diagnostics in Appendix~\ref{app:algorithm}).
HB estimation outperforms stratified MLE in 87.5\% of configurations (21 of 24) across the experimental grid (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}), with the largest gains when $n_{\text{expert}} / K < 100$.
The advantage requires $n_{\text{expert}} \times P(Z_{\text{minority}}) / K \geq 25$ per subgroup; below this threshold, stratified MLE is preferred because the hierarchical model lacks sufficient observations for stable shrinkage.
At $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 1000$, HB and stratified MLE converge to within 0.5\% on all metrics.
Sensitivity analysis shows $<$5\% RMSE variation under 2$\times$ hyperprior perturbation, confirming that results are not driven by prior specification.

\subsection{Subgroup-Stratified Correction}

Given posterior mean confusion matrices $\hat{C}_s$, we correct observed outcome moments per subgroup by matrix inversion:
\begin{equation}
\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s = \hat{C}_s^{-1} \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s,
\end{equation}
where $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s = [\hat{\tau}_{\text{obs}}(0, s),\, \hat{\tau}_{\text{obs}}(1, s)]^\top$ collects the observed conditional outcome moments in subgroup $s$.
This requires $\det(\hat{C}_s) \neq 0$ for all $s$, which holds under assumption~(A4) ($\pi_s \neq 0.5$) but may fail in finite samples when error rates approach degeneracy.
In practice, Laplace smoothing of the confusion matrix counts ensures finite-sample invertibility.
We impose a singularity guard: if the condition number $\kappa(\hat{C}_s) > 100$ (for a $2{\times}2$ symmetric confusion matrix, this corresponds to $\pi_s > 0.495$, i.e., near-random classification), subgroup $s$ falls back to global correction $\bar{C}^{-1}$; when the fallback triggers, the standard error computation also uses $\bar{C}^{-1}$ for that subgroup, ensuring consistency between point estimates and confidence intervals.
This hard guard prevents numerical catastrophe; $\kappa \leq 1.25$ is a sufficient condition for strongest bias reduction (Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}), though EC-HTE maintains calibrated coverage ($\geq$93\%) across the wider $\kappa \in [1.4, 3.0]$ range observed in practice (Appendix~\ref{app:kappa_analysis}).

The contrast with global correction is direct.
Global correction applies $\bar{C}^{-1}$ uniformly to all subgroups, introducing the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ bias identified in Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}.
Subgroup-stratified correction eliminates this bias by matching each subgroup's correction to its own misclassification structure, at the cost of higher variance from estimating $K$ separate confusion matrices (Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}).

\subsection{Variance-Adjusted CausalForest}

For heterogeneous treatment effect estimation, we feed corrected covariates into CausalForestDML~\cite{wager2018causal} with honest splitting.
The forest produces per-observation standard error estimates $\text{se}_i$.
To account for confusion matrix correction, we propagate uncertainty through the inverse mapping:
\begin{equation}
\text{se}_{\text{corrected},i} = \sqrt{\text{diag}\!\left(\hat{C}_{S_i}^{-1}\, \text{diag}(\text{se}_i^2)\, \hat{C}_{S_i}^{-\top}\right)}.
\end{equation}
This plug-in SE conditions on $\hat{C}_s$, neglecting CM estimation uncertainty; at $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 100$ this is negligible, but below this threshold a full bootstrap ($B{=}100$; re-estimate CM and re-fit per replicate) maintains $\geq$95\% coverage across all budgets tested ($n_{\text{expert}} \in \{25, 50, 75, 100, 200\}$); even plug-in SE achieves $\geq$91\% at $n_{\text{expert}}{=}25$ (Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_se}).
When $n_{\text{expert}}/K < 50$, we recommend bootstrap SE; otherwise plug-in SE suffices.

\paragraph{Diagnostic criterion.}
Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts} provides a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic: global correction harms subgroup $s$ if and only if $|\delta_s| / ((1-2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s) > 1$, a condition depending only on per-subgroup misclassification rates estimable from a pilot sample.
This breaks the circular dependency that would arise if the diagnostic required CATE estimates.
A threshold classifier achieves AUC~=~0.86 at the subgroup level, reaching 1.0 when restricted to subgroups with $\tau_s > 0$ (Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).

\paragraph{Composition with PPCI.}
EC-HTE corrects structured covariate misclassification through $\hat{C}_s^{-1}$ inversion but cannot address outcome-level measurement error.
PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} corrects residual outcome bias using a debiasing estimator but assumes correct covariate labels.
The two methods are complementary: apply EC-HTE first to correct covariate labels, then PPCI to correct outcome predictions.
Neither is redundant with the other: EC-HTE alone cannot fix outcome error, while PPCI alone incurs higher variance for covariate error.
Under both error types simultaneously, the composition reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.179 to 0.007 (Appendix~\ref{sec:ppci}).

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Large language models (LLMs) now routinely replace human annotators in computational social science (CSS), producing labels for sentiment, hate speech, stance, and political discourse at costs orders of magnitude below manual coding~\cite{gilardi2023chatgpt,tornberg2024chatgpt,ziems2024nlp}.
When these labels serve as effect modifiers in heterogeneous treatment effect (HTE) analysis, the standard correction protocol\footnote{Throughout, ``debiasing'' refers to correction of annotation measurement-error bias, not algorithmic fairness debiasing.} is straightforward: validate a sample against expert annotations, estimate a confusion matrix, and apply its inverse uniformly to correct conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimates.
Yet LLM annotations are not uniformly accurate: \citet{ashwin2025bias} document misclassification rates varying by up to 5$\times$ across demographic subgroups defined by refugee status, gender, and education level; in our pilot study, GPT-4.1 achieves 85.8\% accuracy on TweetEval sentiment, but error rates range from 10.2\% to 20.0\% across text-feature subgroups ($\Delta\pi = 0.098$).

We show that this standard correction can make things worse.
In 92\% of our 546 synthetic configurations, global correction reverses the sign of the estimated treatment effect for at least one subgroup, directing resources toward communities that benefit least (Figure~\ref{fig:sign_reversal}); all eight real LLMs tested exhibit sign reversal in 49\% of subgroup estimates, while EC-HTE eliminates it entirely.
Global correction amplifies bias by up to 5.9$\times$ ($K{=}4$ with CausalForest); the classical Frazis-Loeb scalar attenuation correction~\cite{frazis2003estimating} \emph{increases} bias by up to 2.9$\times$.
The mechanism is over-correction: for subgroups with near-zero misclassification, the naive estimator is nearly unbiased, yet pooled correction calibrated for the average error rate introduces substantial bias precisely where labels were most trustworthy.

We derive an exact bias identity explaining when and why this occurs (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}): the correction-induced bias in each subgroup factors into three independently estimable components, verified empirically at $R^2 \geq 0.97$ on synthetic grids and $R^2 = 0.975$ across 11 real LLM confusion matrices spanning open-source and proprietary model families.
The identity yields a diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}) that predicts when global correction will harm a subgroup using only per-subgroup misclassification rates, without estimating any treatment effects (AUC $= 1.0$ on subgroups with non-zero effect heterogeneity; Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).

Error-Corrected Heterogeneous Treatment Effects (EC-HTE), the per-subgroup correction prescribed by the identity, reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 to 0.008 under extreme heterogeneity ($K{=}2$) via hierarchical Bayesian confusion matrix estimation.
EC-HTE's advantage is conditional on sufficient error heterogeneity and expert budget; when $\Delta\pi$ is small, the variance cost of stratification outweighs its bias benefit.

Existing corrections---PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi}, DSL~\cite{egami2024dsl}, PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci}, arm-specific PPI~\cite{mozer2026ppi}, ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv}---address population-level or outcome-side measurement error but assume homogeneous prediction error across subgroups; none corrects bias when the mismeasured variable is the effect modifier indexing the CATE function (Section~\ref{sec:related}).

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig1_sign_reversal.pdf}
\caption{Sign reversal under global correction ($K{=}2$, 546 configurations). (A) Naive vs.\ global-corrected bias; red triangles mark sign reversals (50\% of subgroup estimates). (B) Three extreme cases. (C) Summary: 92\% of configurations and all 8 real LLMs exhibit reversal; EC-HTE: 0\%.}
\label{fig:sign_reversal}
\end{figure*}

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
    \item A demonstration that standard confusion-matrix correction---the default in PPI, DSL, and CSS practice---reverses the sign of estimated treatment effects in 92\% of configurations and in all eight real LLMs tested; we derive the first exact finite-population bias decomposition (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) explaining when and why, with multiplicative structure $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1-2\bar{\pi})$, verified at $R^2 \geq 0.97$ on synthetic grids and 11 real LLM confusion matrices (Sections~\ref{sec:theory},~\ref{sec:bias_mechanism}).
    \item An actionable diagnostic derived from the decomposition (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}): a condition on per-subgroup misclassification rates alone predicts when global correction increases bias, achieving AUC $= 1.0$ on subgroups with non-zero effect heterogeneity---independently useful without adopting EC-HTE (Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
    \item EC-HTE, an end-to-end correction pipeline: the bias decomposition identifies the correction target, the diagnostic flags when correction is needed, and hierarchical Bayesian confusion matrix estimation executes per-subgroup correction---compatible with difference-in-means, CausalForest, and R-learner, and composable with PPCI for joint covariate/outcome error (Sections~\ref{sec:method}--\ref{sec:diagnostic}; Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}).
\end{itemize}
While we develop the theory and experiments for LLM annotation---the leading practical case---the bias identity applies whenever any proxy classifier with subgroup-varying error rates is used to construct effect modifiers for causal inference.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Consider estimating whether a content moderation policy reduces hate speech differently across demographic groups, using GPT-4 to classify thousands of posts.
After standard confusion-matrix correction, the analysis concludes the policy \emph{increases} hate speech among younger users---but the true effect is protective.
This sign reversal is not an edge case.

Large language models (LLMs) now routinely replace human annotators in computational social science (CSS), producing labels for sentiment, hate speech, stance, and political discourse at costs orders of magnitude below manual coding~\cite{gilardi2023chatgpt,tornberg2024chatgpt,ziems2024nlp}.
When these labels serve as effect modifiers in heterogeneous treatment effect (HTE) analysis, the standard correction protocol\footnote{Throughout, ``debiasing'' refers to correction of annotation measurement-error bias, not algorithmic fairness debiasing.} is straightforward: validate a sample against expert annotations, estimate a confusion matrix, and apply its inverse uniformly to correct conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimates.
Yet LLM annotations are not uniformly accurate: \citet{ashwin2025bias} document misclassification rates varying by up to 5$\times$ across demographic subgroups defined by refugee status, gender, and education level; in our pilot study, GPT-4.1 achieves 85.8\% accuracy on TweetEval sentiment, but error rates range from 10.2\% to 20.0\% across text-feature subgroups ($\Delta\pi = 0.098$).

We show that this standard correction can make things worse.
In 92\% of our 546 synthetic configurations, global correction reverses the sign of the estimated treatment effect for at least one subgroup, directing resources toward communities that benefit least (Figure~\ref{fig:sign_reversal}); all eight real LLMs tested exhibit sign reversal in 49\% of subgroup estimates, while EC-HTE eliminates it entirely.
Global correction amplifies bias by up to 5.9$\times$ ($K{=}4$ with CausalForest); the classical Frazis-Loeb scalar attenuation correction~\cite{frazis2003estimating} \emph{increases} bias by up to 2.9$\times$.
The mechanism is over-correction: for subgroups with near-zero misclassification, the naive estimator is nearly unbiased, yet pooled correction calibrated for the average error rate introduces substantial bias precisely where labels were most trustworthy.

We derive an exact bias identity explaining when and why this occurs (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}): the correction-induced bias in each subgroup factors into three independently estimable components, verified empirically at $R^2 \geq 0.97$ on synthetic grids and $R^2 = 0.975$ across 11 real LLM confusion matrices spanning open-source and proprietary model families.
The identity yields a diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}) that predicts when global correction will harm a subgroup using only per-subgroup misclassification rates, without estimating any treatment effects (AUC $= 1.0$ on subgroups with non-zero effect heterogeneity; Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).

Error-Corrected Heterogeneous Treatment Effects (EC-HTE), the per-subgroup correction prescribed by the identity, reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 to 0.008 under extreme heterogeneity ($K{=}2$) via hierarchical Bayesian confusion matrix estimation.
EC-HTE's advantage is conditional on sufficient error heterogeneity and expert budget; when $\Delta\pi$ is small, the variance cost of stratification outweighs its bias benefit.

Existing corrections---PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi}, DSL~\cite{egami2024dsl}, PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci}, arm-specific PPI~\cite{mozer2026ppi}, ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv}---assume homogeneous prediction error; none addresses effect modifier misclassification (Section~\ref{sec:related}).

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig1_sign_reversal.pdf}
\caption{Sign reversal under global correction ($K{=}2$, 546 configurations). (A) Naive vs.\ global-corrected bias; red triangles mark sign reversals (50\% of subgroup estimates). (B) Three extreme cases. (C) Summary: 92\% of configurations and all 8 real LLMs exhibit reversal; EC-HTE: 0\%.}
\label{fig:sign_reversal}
\end{figure*}

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
    \item A demonstration that standard confusion-matrix correction---the default in PPI, DSL, and CSS practice---reverses the sign of estimated treatment effects in 92\% of configurations and in all eight real LLMs tested; we derive the first exact finite-population bias decomposition (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) explaining when and why, with multiplicative structure $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1-2\bar{\pi})$, verified at $R^2 \geq 0.97$ on synthetic grids and 11 real LLM confusion matrices (Sections~\ref{sec:theory},~\ref{sec:bias_mechanism}).
    \item An actionable diagnostic derived from the decomposition (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}): a condition on per-subgroup misclassification rates alone predicts when global correction increases bias, achieving AUC $= 1.0$ on subgroups with non-zero effect heterogeneity---independently useful without adopting EC-HTE (Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
    \item EC-HTE, an end-to-end correction pipeline: the bias decomposition identifies the correction target, the diagnostic flags when correction is needed, and hierarchical Bayesian confusion matrix estimation executes per-subgroup correction---compatible with difference-in-means, CausalForest, and R-learner, and composable with PPCI for joint covariate/outcome error (Sections~\ref{sec:method}--\ref{sec:diagnostic}; Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}).
\end{itemize}
While we develop the theory and experiments for LLM annotation---the leading practical case---the bias identity applies whenever any proxy classifier with subgroup-varying error rates is used to construct effect modifiers for causal inference.

Yes. The Limitations section (after Section 6) discusses: (1) expert budget thresholds per subgroup, (2) RMSE variance cost at K=4 with small n, (3) baseline classifier accuracy requirements, (4) plug-in SE vs bootstrap coverage calibration, (5) untestable A1 assumption with sensitivity analysis, (6) diagnostic AUC degradation on real CMs, (7) symmetric/additive assumptions with robustness checks, (8) discrete pre-defined subgroup requirement.

**B. Did you discuss any potential risks of your work?**
Yes. We discuss conditions under which EC-HTE should NOT be applied (low error heterogeneity, insufficient expert budget, K=8 boundary), preventing misuse of stratified correction. The diagnostic criterion (Proposition 3) guards against inappropriate application.

**C. Do the abstract and introduction summarize the paper's main claims?**
Yes. The abstract states three contributions (bias identity, diagnostic, EC-HTE method) with quantitative results. The introduction provides a numbered contribution list (page 2).

Yes. Both datasets used as research benchmarks for semi-synthetic CATE experiments.

Not applicable. No human participants. Expert labels in semi-synthetic experiments are simulated from known ground truth.

Yes. Primary risk is applying EC-HTE when assumptions are violated. The diagnostic criterion and Limitations section guard against inappropriate application.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Consider estimating whether a content moderation policy reduces hate speech differently across demographic groups, using GPT-4 to classify thousands of posts.
After standard confusion-matrix correction, the analysis concludes the policy \emph{increases} hate speech among younger users---but the true effect is protective.
This sign reversal is not an edge case.

Large language models (LLMs) now routinely replace human annotators in computational social science (CSS), producing labels for sentiment, hate speech, stance, and political discourse at costs orders of magnitude below manual coding~\cite{gilardi2023chatgpt,tornberg2024chatgpt,ziems2024nlp}.
When these labels serve as effect modifiers in heterogeneous treatment effect (HTE) analysis, the standard correction protocol\footnote{Throughout, ``debiasing'' refers to correction of annotation measurement-error bias, not algorithmic fairness debiasing.} is straightforward: validate a sample against expert annotations, estimate a confusion matrix, and apply its inverse uniformly to correct conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimates.
Yet LLM annotations are not uniformly accurate: \citet{ashwin2025bias} document misclassification rates varying by up to 5$\times$ across demographic subgroups defined by refugee status, gender, and education level; in our pilot study, GPT-4.1 achieves 85.8\% accuracy on TweetEval sentiment, but error rates range from 10.2\% to 20.0\% across text-feature subgroups ($\Delta\pi = 0.098$).

We show that this standard correction can make things worse.
In 92\% of our 546 synthetic configurations, global correction reverses the sign of the estimated treatment effect for at least one subgroup, directing resources toward communities that benefit least (Figure~\ref{fig:sign_reversal}); all eight real LLMs tested exhibit sign reversal in 49\% of subgroup estimates, while EC-HTE eliminates it entirely.
Global correction amplifies bias by up to 5.9$\times$ ($K{=}4$ with CausalForest); the classical Frazis-Loeb scalar attenuation correction~\cite{frazis2003estimating} \emph{increases} bias by up to 2.9$\times$.
The mechanism is over-correction: for subgroups with near-zero misclassification, the naive estimator is nearly unbiased, yet pooled correction calibrated for the average error rate introduces substantial bias precisely where labels were most trustworthy.

We derive an exact bias identity explaining when and why this occurs (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}): the correction-induced bias in each subgroup factors into three independently estimable components, verified empirically at $R^2 \geq 0.97$ on synthetic grids and $R^2 = 0.975$ across 11 real LLM confusion matrices spanning open-source and proprietary model families.
The identity yields a diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}) that predicts when global correction will harm a subgroup using only per-subgroup misclassification rates, without estimating any treatment effects (AUC $= 1.0$ on subgroups with non-zero effect heterogeneity; Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).

Error-Corrected Heterogeneous Treatment Effects (EC-HTE), the per-subgroup correction prescribed by the identity, reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 to 0.008 under extreme heterogeneity ($K{=}2$) via hierarchical Bayesian confusion matrix estimation.
EC-HTE's advantage is conditional on sufficient error heterogeneity and expert budget; when $\Delta\pi$ is small, the variance cost of stratification outweighs its bias benefit.

Existing corrections---PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi}, DSL~\cite{egami2024dsl}, PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci}, arm-specific PPI~\cite{mozer2026ppi}, ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv}---assume homogeneous prediction error; none addresses effect modifier misclassification (Section~\ref{sec:related}).

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig1_sign_reversal.pdf}
\caption{Sign reversal under global correction ($K{=}2$, 546 configurations). (A) Naive vs.\ global-corrected bias; red triangles mark sign reversals (50\% of subgroup estimates). (B) Three extreme cases. (C) Summary: 92\% of configurations and all 8 real LLMs exhibit reversal; EC-HTE: 0\%.}
\label{fig:sign_reversal}
\end{figure*}

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
    \item A demonstration that standard confusion-matrix correction---the default in PPI, DSL, and CSS practice---reverses the sign of estimated treatment effects in 92\% of configurations and in all eight real LLMs tested; we derive the first exact finite-population bias decomposition (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) explaining when and why, with multiplicative structure $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1-2\bar{\pi})$, verified at $R^2 \geq 0.97$ on synthetic grids and 11 real LLM confusion matrices (Sections~\ref{sec:theory},~\ref{sec:bias_mechanism}).
    \item An actionable diagnostic derived from the decomposition (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}): a condition on per-subgroup misclassification rates alone predicts when global correction increases bias, achieving AUC $= 1.0$ on subgroups with non-zero effect heterogeneity---independently useful without adopting EC-HTE (Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
    \item EC-HTE, an end-to-end correction pipeline: the bias decomposition identifies the correction target, the diagnostic flags when correction is needed, and hierarchical Bayesian confusion matrix estimation executes per-subgroup correction---compatible with difference-in-means, CausalForest, and R-learner, and composable with PPCI for joint covariate/outcome error (Sections~\ref{sec:method}--\ref{sec:diagnostic}; Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}).
\end{itemize}

2	
3	\subsection{Setup}
4	
5	We test on synthetic ($N{=}5{,}000$, $K \in \{2, 4\}$, controlled $\Delta\tau$ and $\Delta\pi$, 100 MC runs) and semi-synthetic (TweetEval sentiment~\cite{barbieri2020tweeteval}, $K{=}4$ unbalanced subgroups, $\pi \in \{0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.25\}$) DGPs; full specifications in Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}.
6	
7	We compare: (1) \textit{Naive} (no correction), (2) \textit{Global} (pooled confusion matrix, equivalent to PPI/DSL~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi,egami2024dsl} with homogeneous error), (3) \textit{Stratified MLE} (per-subgroup DSL without shrinkage), (4) \textit{HB EC-HTE} (our method), (5) \textit{PPCI}~\cite{sui2026ppci}, and (6) \textit{EC-HTE+PPCI}.
8	For CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal}, we compare naive, global, and EC-HTE variants.
9	Primary metrics are $|\text{bias}|$, RMSE, and 95\% CI coverage, averaged across subgroups and 100 MC runs.
10	Robustness validation covers hate speech, six OpenAI models, subgroup misspecification, asymmetric confusion matrices, confounded treatment, and outcome-dependent misclassification (all $\geq$93.5\% coverage; Appendices~\ref{app:hatespeech}--\ref{app:a1_sensitivity}).
11	
12	\subsection{Empirical Validation of the Bias Identity}
13	\label{sec:bias_mechanism}
14	
15	We verify Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} on a $K{=}2$ grid (520 configurations, $\Delta\pi \in [0, 0.25]$, $\Delta\tau \in (0, 0.50]$) and a $K{=}4$ grid (Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}).
16	Regressing observed subgroup bias on $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1{-}2\bar{\pi})$ yields $R^2 = 0.994$ ($K{=}2$) and $0.974$ ($K{=}4$); residual variance reflects MC noise ($R^2 \geq 0.976$ even at $P(Z{=}1) = 0.1$; Appendix~\ref{app:classimbalance}).
17	Global correction worsens bias in 50\% of $K{=}2$ configurations (260/520, excluding $\Delta\pi{=}0$), with amplification reaching 2.86$\times$ ($K{=}2$) and 2.41$\times$ ($K{=}4$); Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} visualizes the amplification surface.
18	Beyond amplification, global correction reverses the sign of the estimated treatment effect for at least one subgroup in 92\% of configurations (500/546, 50\% of all subgroup-rows), with all eight real LLMs exhibiting the same pattern (49\%); EC-HTE eliminates sign reversal entirely (Figure~\ref{fig:sign_reversal}).
19	
20	\begin{figure*}[t]
21	\centering
22	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig2_heatmap.pdf}
23	\caption{Bias amplification under global correction ($K{=}2$). (a) Low-error subgroup: correction always helps. (b) High-error subgroup: correction \emph{increases} bias when $\Delta\pi > 0.12$ (hatched), reaching 2.86$\times$.}
24	\label{fig:heatmap}
25	\end{figure*}
26	
27	\subsection{EC-HTE Evaluation}
28	\label{sec:ec_hte_eval}
29	
30	Table~\ref{tab:main_results} presents the main results across representative configurations.
31	In the $K{=}2$ extreme row, global correction \emph{increases} $|\text{bias}|$ relative to naive (0.059 vs.\ 0.058), confirming the over-correction mechanism of Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}.
32	F-L scalar correction ($\hat{\tau}/(1{-}2\bar{\pi})$) increases $|\text{bias}|$ to 0.122 with coverage 0.68---worse than naive---because a single scalar cannot correct heterogeneous attenuation; F-L per-subgroup inflates bias to 0.168 as $(1{-}2\pi_s) \to 0$ (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}).
33	HB EC-HTE reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 to 0.008 (7.4$\times$) at $K{=}2$ and from 0.056 to 0.012 (4.7$\times$) at $K{=}4$, maintaining near-nominal coverage (0.94--0.96) with lower RMSE than stratified MLE.
34	Under moderate heterogeneity ($K{=}2$) and in the semi-synthetic TweetEval experiment ($K{=}4$, $n_{\text{expert}}{=}250$), methods converge: EC-HTE and global achieve comparable bias ($p > 0.05$), though EC-HTE incurs higher RMSE when $\Delta\pi$ or per-subgroup budget is marginal (Table~\ref{tab:main_supp}).
35	
36	\paragraph{CausalForest.}
37	With CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal} ($K{=}4$, extreme, $n{=}500$), EC-HTE reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.191 to 0.039 (4.9$\times$), improving coverage from 0.58 to 0.90; global correction amplifies naive bias up to 5.9$\times$ because the forest magnifies label errors (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}).
38	The residual coverage gap (90\% vs.\ oracle 94--96\%) reflects $M^{-1}$ SE propagation; a full bootstrap corrects this (Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_se}).
39

41	\centering
42	\caption{Main results (extreme heterogeneity). Metrics averaged over subgroups, $z$-levels, 100 MC runs. Bold: lowest $|\text{bias}|$. $^\dagger$RMSE exceeds Global. 71	\subsection{Actionable Diagnostic Without EC-HTE}
72	\label{sec:diagnostic}
73	
74	Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts} provides a $\Delta\tau$-free diagnostic: global correction increases bias in subgroup $s$ iff $|\delta_s| / ((1-2\bar{\pi}) \cdot \pi_s) > 1$, computable from a pilot sample without estimating treatment effects.
75	A threshold classifier achieves AUC = 0.86 at the subgroup level (Figure~\ref{fig:roc}, Appendix).
76	On real LLM confusion matrices (16 combinations; Appendix~\ref{app:screening}), AUC drops to 0.63; restricting to subgroups with $\tau_s > 0$ recovers AUC $= 1.0$.
77	For $K{=}2$, $|\delta_0|{=}|\delta_1|$ limits discrimination; a meta-criterion ($\max_s \mathrm{score}(s) > 1$) recovers reliability (AUC $\geq 0.75$) for $K{\geq}4$, while $\max_s \mathrm{score}(s) \leq 1$ signals unreliable regimes (Appendix~\ref{app:screening}).
78	
79	The condition number $\kappa(\hat{C}_s)$ governs correction at three levels: $\kappa > 100$ triggers the singularity guard; $\kappa \leq 1.25$ guarantees strongest bias reduction; $\kappa \in (1.25, 3]$---covering all 13 tested LLM--dataset combinations---maintains calibrated coverage ($\geq$93\% vs.\ Global 86--91\%) with RMSE gains at $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 500$ (Appendix~\ref{app:kappa_analysis}).
80	Budget crossover curves, $K{=}8$ scalability, and multi-LLM validation ($R^2 = 0.975$) appear in Appendices~\ref{sec:budget}--\ref{app:multilm}.

\begin{abstract}
Standard confusion-matrix correction for noisy annotations assumes uniform error rates.
When this assumption fails, correction can increase rather than decrease bias in heterogeneous treatment effect (HTE) estimates, reversing the sign of estimated effect heterogeneity.
LLMs, now widely used as proxy classifiers in computational social science, are the leading practical instance, with error rates varying by up to $5\times$ across demographic subgroups.
We derive the first exact bias decomposition for this setting: global correction introduces subgroup-level bias with a product form factoring into each subgroup's deviation from the pooled error rate, the treatment effect heterogeneity, and an amplification factor from matrix inversion.
This is not a bound but a population-level identity; global correction reverses the sign of estimated treatment effects for at least one subgroup in 92\% of configurations, and in all eight real LLMs tested.
The decomposition yields a diagnostic that predicts harmful correction from per-subgroup error rates alone (AUC $= 1.0$ on subgroups with non-zero effect heterogeneity).
Error-Corrected Heterogeneous Treatment Effects (EC-HTE), the per-subgroup correction prescribed by the decomposition, reduces $|\text{bias}|$ by $7.4\times$ under extreme heterogeneity with coverage $\geq 0.90$ via hierarchical Bayesian estimation; the advantage requires sufficient error heterogeneity and expert budget.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Consider estimating whether a content moderation policy reduces hate speech differently across demographic groups, using GPT-4 to classify thousands of posts.
After standard confusion-matrix correction, the analysis concludes the policy \emph{increases} hate speech among younger users---but the true effect is protective.
This sign reversal is not an edge case.

Large language models (LLMs) now routinely replace human annotators in computational social science (CSS), producing labels for sentiment, hate speech, stance, and political discourse at costs orders of magnitude below manual coding~\cite{gilardi2023chatgpt,tornberg2024chatgpt,ziems2024nlp}.
When these labels serve as effect modifiers in heterogeneous treatment effect (HTE) analysis, the standard correction protocol\footnote{Throughout, ``debiasing'' refers to correction of annotation measurement-error bias, not algorithmic fairness debiasing.} is straightforward: validate a sample against expert annotations, estimate a confusion matrix, and apply its inverse uniformly to correct conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimates.
Yet LLM annotations are not uniformly accurate: \citet{ashwin2025bias} document misclassification rates varying by up to 5$\times$ across demographic subgroups defined by refugee status, gender, and education level; in our pilot study, GPT-4.1 achieves 85.8\% accuracy on TweetEval sentiment, but error rates range from 10.2\% to 20.0\% across text-feature subgroups ($\Delta\pi = 0.098$).

We show that this standard correction can make things worse.
In 92\% of our 546 synthetic configurations, global correction reverses the sign of the estimated treatment effect for at least one subgroup, directing resources toward communities that benefit least (Figure~\ref{fig:sign_reversal}); all eight real LLMs tested exhibit sign reversal in 49\% of subgroup estimates, while EC-HTE eliminates it entirely.
Global correction amplifies bias by up to 5.9$\times$ ($K{=}4$ with CausalForest); the classical Frazis-Loeb scalar attenuation correction~\cite{frazis2003estimating} \emph{increases} bias by up to 2.9$\times$.
The mechanism is over-correction: for subgroups with near-zero misclassification, the naive estimator is nearly unbiased, yet pooled correction calibrated for the average error rate introduces substantial bias precisely where labels were most trustworthy.

We derive an exact bias identity explaining when and why this occurs (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}): the correction-induced bias in each subgroup factors into three independently estimable components, verified empirically at $R^2 \geq 0.97$ on synthetic grids and $R^2 = 0.975$ across 11 real LLM confusion matrices spanning open-source and proprietary model families.
The identity yields a diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}) that predicts when global correction will harm a subgroup using only per-subgroup misclassification rates, without estimating any treatment effects (AUC $= 1.0$ on subgroups with non-zero effect heterogeneity; Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).

Error-Corrected Heterogeneous Treatment Effects (EC-HTE), the per-subgroup correction prescribed by the identity, reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 to 0.008 under extreme heterogeneity ($K{=}2$) via hierarchical Bayesian confusion matrix estimation.
EC-HTE's advantage is conditional on sufficient error heterogeneity and expert budget; when $\Delta\pi$ is small, the variance cost of stratification outweighs its bias benefit.

Existing corrections---PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi}, DSL~\cite{egami2024dsl}, PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci}, arm-specific PPI~\cite{mozer2026ppi}, ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv}---assume homogeneous prediction error; none addresses effect modifier misclassification (Section~\ref{sec:related}).

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig1_sign_reversal.pdf}
\caption{Sign reversal under global correction ($K{=}2$, 546 configurations). (A) Naive vs.\ global-corrected bias; red triangles mark sign reversals (50\% of subgroup estimates). (B) Three extreme cases. (C) Summary: 92\% of configurations and all 8 real LLMs exhibit reversal; EC-HTE: 0\%.}
\label{fig:sign_reversal}
\end{figure*}

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
    \item A demonstration that standard confusion-matrix correction---the default in PPI, DSL, and CSS practice---reverses the sign of estimated treatment effects in 92\% of configurations and in all eight real LLMs tested; we derive the first exact finite-population bias decomposition (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) explaining when and why, with multiplicative structure $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1-2\bar{\pi})$, verified at $R^2 \geq 0.97$ on synthetic grids and 11 real LLM confusion matrices (Sections~\ref{sec:theory},~\ref{sec:bias_mechanism}).
    \item An actionable diagnostic derived from the decomposition (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}): a condition on per-subgroup misclassification rates alone predicts when global correction increases bias, achieving AUC $= 1.0$ on subgroups with non-zero effect heterogeneity---independently useful without adopting EC-HTE (Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
    \item EC-HTE, an end-to-end correction pipeline: the bias decomposition identifies the correction target, the diagnostic flags when correction is needed, and hierarchical Bayesian confusion matrix estimation executes per-subgroup correction---compatible with difference-in-means, CausalForest, and R-learner, and composable with PPCI for joint covariate/outcome error (Sections~\ref{sec:method}--\ref{sec:diagnostic}; Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}).
\end{itemize}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Consider estimating whether a content moderation policy reduces hate speech differently across demographic groups, using GPT-4 to classify thousands of posts.
After standard confusion-matrix correction, the analysis concludes the policy \emph{increases} hate speech among younger users---but the true effect is protective.
This sign reversal is not an edge case.

Large language models (LLMs) now routinely replace human annotators in computational social science (CSS), producing labels for sentiment, hate speech, stance, and political discourse at costs orders of magnitude below manual coding~\cite{gilardi2023chatgpt,tornberg2024chatgpt,ziems2024nlp}.
When these labels serve as effect modifiers in heterogeneous treatment effect (HTE) analysis, the standard correction protocol\footnote{Throughout, ``debiasing'' refers to correction of annotation measurement-error bias, not algorithmic fairness debiasing.} is straightforward: validate a sample against expert annotations, estimate a confusion matrix, and apply its inverse uniformly to correct conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimates.
Yet LLM annotations are not uniformly accurate: \citet{ashwin2025bias} document misclassification rates varying by up to 5$\times$ across demographic subgroups defined by refugee status, gender, and education level; in our pilot study, GPT-4.1 achieves 85.8\% accuracy on TweetEval sentiment, but error rates range from 10.2\% to 20.0\% across text-feature subgroups ($\Delta\pi = 0.098$).

We show that this standard correction can make things worse.
In {\bfseries[XX]\%} of our synthetic configurations, global correction reverses the sign of the estimated CATE for at least one subgroup, directing resources toward communities that benefit least (Figure~\ref{fig:sign_reversal}); all eight real LLMs tested exhibit sign reversal in {\bfseries[YY]\%} of subgroup estimates, while EC-HTE eliminates it entirely.
Global correction amplifies bias by up to 5.9$\times$ ($K{=}4$ with CausalForest); the classical Frazis-Loeb scalar attenuation correction~\cite{frazis2003estimating} \emph{increases} bias by up to 2.9$\times$.
The mechanism is over-correction: for subgroups with near-zero misclassification, the naive estimator is nearly unbiased, yet pooled correction calibrated for the average error rate introduces substantial bias precisely where labels were most trustworthy.

We derive an exact bias identity explaining when and why this occurs (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}): the correction-induced bias in each subgroup factors into three independently estimable components, verified empirically at $R^2 \geq 0.97$ on synthetic grids and $R^2 = 0.975$ across 11 real LLM confusion matrices spanning open-source and proprietary model families.
The identity yields a diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}) that predicts when global correction will harm a subgroup using only per-subgroup misclassification rates, without estimating any treatment effects (AUC $= 1.0$ on subgroups with non-zero effect heterogeneity; Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).

Error-Corrected Heterogeneous Treatment Effects (EC-HTE), the per-subgroup correction prescribed by the identity, reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 to 0.008 under extreme heterogeneity ($K{=}2$) via hierarchical Bayesian confusion matrix estimation.
EC-HTE's advantage is conditional on sufficient error heterogeneity and expert budget; when $\Delta\pi$ is small, the variance cost of stratification outweighs its bias benefit.

Existing corrections---PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi}, DSL~\cite{egami2024dsl}, PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci}, arm-specific PPI~\cite{mozer2026ppi}, ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv}---assume homogeneous prediction error; none addresses effect modifier misclassification (Section~\ref{sec:related}).

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig1_sign_reversal.pdf}
\caption{Sign reversal under global correction ($K{=}2$, 546 configurations). (A) Naive vs.\ global-corrected bias; red triangles mark sign reversals (50\% of subgroup estimates). (B) Three extreme cases. (C) Summary: 92\% of configurations and all 8 real LLMs exhibit reversal; EC-HTE: 0\%.}
\label{fig:sign_reversal}
\end{figure*}

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
    \item A demonstration that standard confusion-matrix correction---the default in PPI, DSL, and CSS practice---can reverse the sign of estimated CATE in {\bfseries[XX]\%} of configurations and in all eight real LLMs tested; we derive the first exact finite-population bias decomposition (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) explaining when and why, with multiplicative structure $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1-2\bar{\pi})$, verified at $R^2 \geq 0.97$ on synthetic grids and 11 real LLM confusion matrices (Sections~\ref{sec:theory},~\ref{sec:bias_mechanism}).
    \item An actionable diagnostic derived from the decomposition (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}): a condition on per-subgroup misclassification rates alone predicts when global correction increases bias, achieving AUC $= 1.0$ on subgroups with non-zero effect heterogeneity---independently useful without adopting EC-HTE (Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
    \item EC-HTE, an end-to-end correction pipeline: the bias decomposition identifies the correction target, the diagnostic flags when correction is needed, and hierarchical Bayesian confusion matrix estimation executes per-subgroup correction---compatible with difference-in-means, CausalForest, and R-learner, and composable with PPCI for joint covariate/outcome error (Sections~\ref{sec:method}--\ref{sec:diagnostic}; Appendix~\ref{sec:budget}).
\end{itemize}

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We derived a bias identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}): global confusion-matrix correction introduces bias proportional to $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$, reversing treatment effect signs in 92\% of configurations and all eight real LLMs tested.
EC-HTE eliminates sign reversal via hierarchical Bayesian subgroup correction; the diagnostic (Proposition~\ref{prop:debiasing_hurts}; AUC $= 1.0$ on subgroups with $\tau_s > 0$) flags harmful correction from error rates alone.
The advantage requires sufficient $\Delta\pi$ and expert budget; the identity applies to any proxy classifier with subgroup-varying error rates.

\begin{abstract}
Standard confusion-matrix correction for noisy annotations assumes uniform error rates.
When this assumption fails, correction can increase rather than decrease bias in heterogeneous treatment effect (HTE) estimates, reversing the sign of estimated effect heterogeneity.
LLMs, now widely used as proxy classifiers in computational social science, are the leading practical instance, with error rates varying by up to $5\times$ across demographic subgroups.
We derive the first exact bias decomposition for this setting: global correction introduces subgroup-level bias with a product form factoring into each subgroup's deviation from the pooled error rate, the treatment effect heterogeneity, and an amplification factor from matrix inversion.
This is not a bound but a population-level identity; global correction can reverse the sign of estimated treatment effects for at least one subgroup in {\bfseries[XX]\%} of configurations, and in all eight real LLMs tested.
The decomposition yields a diagnostic that predicts harmful correction from per-subgroup error rates alone (AUC $= 1.0$ on subgroups with non-zero effect heterogeneity).
Error-Corrected Heterogeneous Treatment Effects (EC-HTE), the per-subgroup correction prescribed by the decomposition, reduces $|\text{bias}|$ by $7.4\times$ under extreme heterogeneity with coverage $\geq 0.90$ via hierarchical Bayesian estimation; the advantage requires sufficient error heterogeneity and expert budget.
\end{abstract}
